Zcash 2026–2027 Reflexive Forecast (paid post)

Source: SightBringer Inner Ring, Oct 27, 2026 (full text pasted by Hunter). His first full forecast on Zcash (ZEC), a privacy-focused cryptocurrency with a 21 million coin cap. Reference price: about $1,290.

The calls

  • End of 2026: about $1,450. Bull 37% ($1,500+), base 37% ($1,000–$1,500, his pick), bear 26% (below $1,000). He's less sure about the next nine weeks than the longer path.
  • End of 2027: about $2,200, with new all-time dollar highs by June 30, 2027. Bull 40% ($1,700+, his pick), base 33% ($1,200–$1,700), bear 27% (below $1,200). At $2,200 ZEC would be worth about $39B, versus about $22B today.

Why he's bullish

  • Privacy is worth more as AI gets better at tracing transactions. Public blockchains leave a permanent money trail; Zcash can hide it. He thinks people may hold ZEC the way they hold gold, for the option, before they actually use it much.
  • Fund buying is back. Grayscale's Zcash fund (ZCSH) drove the September run toward $1,700, then redemptions drove the drop. It just had its first week of net inflows since, going from about 560,800 to 577,400 ZEC (Oct 23–26). Winklevoss filed for a cheaper spot ZEC fund (0.25% fee vs Grayscale's 2.5%) with interest in up to $100M of shares; Bitwise filed for a Zcash strategy fund. Grayscale plus Cypherpunk Technologies (about 332,000 ZEC) already hold over 5% of supply.
  • Supply is small relative to that demand. About 17M coins exist; about 1,800 new coins a day (about $2.3M/day). Getting to 1 million ZEC in US funds would take about 423,000 more coins, roughly 235 days of new supply. Prices move on the last coins traded, so steady buying can push price up more than the dollars going in.
  • About 29% of coins (4.96M) sit in private "shielded" pools, below a 2026 peak of 5.15M. Six million would be a meaningful milestone.

Risks he flags

  • Security: a counterfeit-type bug existed in one private pool from 2022 until a July 28 fix. About 90% of that pool has migrated safely, and the new design is backed by formal proofs, but past abuse can't be fully ruled out.
  • Upgrade: NU7 on Nov 5 cuts block time from 75 to 25 seconds; an Oct 21 checkpoint still had open tasks.
  • Regulation: US is friendlier (SEC closed its Zcash Foundation probe; FinCEN dropped some proposed rules). Europe is tighter, with new anti-money-laundering rules in July 2027.
  • Biggest risk: fund money flows in faster than real long-term holders show up, so rallies get given back like September. Most of the bear case is a broader crypto liquidity drop.

What would change his mind

  • Near term: an official NU7 delay, or two straight weeks of fund outflows after the upgrade.
  • Whole thesis: two straight months of net fund outflows in Q1 2027. Missing new highs by June 30, 2027 counts as a timing miss.
  • He'll track total fund holdings, shielded balances, NU7, new fund launches and EU rules. His key test: how much of the next rally holders refuse to give back.

SEP touch: Hunter doesn't own ZEC and it isn't in the plan, so nothing changes.

SightBringer on X, Oct 27: Zcash forecast launch, AI essays, debt and the ownership class

Source: @The_Prophet_ (16 posts from about 11:58 AM ET Tue Oct 27 to 3:53 AM ET Wed Oct 28, including 2 reposts and several short replies)

New paid post: "Zcash 2026–2027 Reflexive Forecast" (~5:41 PM ET)

He published his first full forecast on Zcash (ZEC), a privacy-focused cryptocurrency, for Inner Ring subscribers only: Zcash 2026–2027 Reflexive Forecast. He says many subscribers had asked for it, that he only forecasts an asset once he understands the forces behind it, and that institutional flows, network fundamentals and a broader shift toward financial privacy made the timing right. In a reply he confirmed it includes price forecasts with the reasoning and scenarios behind them. No numbers are public; he reposted the announcement at ~3:53 AM. Full text needs a paste.

"AI has begun improving the machinery of intelligence itself" (~1:23 PM ET)

Quoting reports that an OpenAI model claims to have disproved a long-standing computer science assumption (the Exponential Time Hypothesis, still under independent review): - AI now helps discover the algorithms that make computing cheaper. Cheaper computing allows more experiments, which lead to more discoveries, a feedback loop. - The first real form of AI self-improvement doesn't need a machine to redesign its successor; it can come from thousands of small discoveries that keep lowering the cost of building and running AI. - How much intelligence you get from a fixed amount of chips and power is becoming a moving target. A company with better algorithms effectively gets more computing power without buying hardware, but cheaper computing also creates new uses, which should still drive demand for more infrastructure. - His conclusion: "intelligence has entered the process of improving its own production function," and that matters more long term than another generation of faster chips.

Debt is now "writing policy" (~8:27 PM ET)

Quoting news that US national debt hit a record $40.5 trillion: - Each extra trillion is a claim on future taxes, growth and monetary policy. At this scale, debt stops adding flexibility and starts consuming it. - The government becomes less able to tolerate high real interest rates, deflation, deep recessions or asset-price crashes, so policy bends around the balance sheet. The US increasingly needs nominal growth just to keep room to maneuver. - That's why AI belongs in the debt conversation: a real productivity jump would grow the economy fast enough to restore breathing room. If not, the adjustment shows up in the currency, lost purchasing power, suppressed interest rates and future taxes. - "The debt problem is ultimately a sovereignty problem."

When you entered the ownership class (~1:37 PM ET)

Quoting a CNBC/ABC finding that Americans under 50 feel far more squeezed by costs than those over 50: owners who bought earlier (for example with low fixed-rate mortgages) get richer from the same forces that make entry harder for newcomers. Falling rates lift asset values for owners; rising rates punish new buyers. AI adds a layer, since capital owners get more productive machines while young workers face uncertainty about their labor. Prosperity increasingly depends on when you entered the ownership class.

Trump and the word "superintelligence" (~1:42 PM ET)

On a Trump statement (he highlights the word "BANNING"): the presidency is calling machines superintelligent before anyone has agreed the threshold has been crossed. Once institutions use that label, questioning the machine starts to feel different from questioning software, and authority shifts toward whoever controls it. He expects a fight between governments and companies over who defines, certifies and controls "superior intelligence." No market call.

Google DeepMind's Genie 4 (~1:46 PM ET)

Genie 4 generates realistic, interactive 3D worlds in real time. His take: AI can now gain "experience" in simulated worlds far faster than physical time allows, and better agents push for better simulated worlds, but simulations can be wrong, so the winners will combine unlimited synthetic experience with constant testing against the real world. No market call.

Short lines

  • "The signal has never asked to be believed. It asks only that someone possess the courage to follow it." (~11:58 AM)
  • "Wow," quoting a Reuters-sourced report that Flavio Bolsonaro fled Brazil for the US (~2:06 PM).
  • A repost of a fan quoting his "production function" line, and Herbert Simon's "a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention" (~3:30 AM).

SEP touch: the debt post restates the debasement case behind the MSTR and ASST amplifiers, and the AI-efficiency post argues cheaper computing still raises demand for chips and data centers, which fits the NVDA anchor. Zcash isn't in the plan; the full forecast is summarized above, and nothing changes.

Educational analysis, not professional financial advice.

title: AI Investor, 10/27: SK Hynix's record quarter, memory makers lock in long-term deals, and his portfolio is back near 100% for the year
html:
Quip: SK Hynix sees memory demand beating supply through 2030

Date: Oct 27, 2026. Patreon Quip (summary via Muse).

SK Hynix repeated that it expects demand for its memory chips to keep running ahead of supply all the way through 2030. It has signed long-term agreements with 14 major customers, and those agreements already cover more than half of its total production capacity for 2027 and 2028. He uses this as an example of why he trusts data over market noise, and points back to his earlier article that projected and stress-tested memory supply and demand. No new trade, position size, or price target.

Quip: China's tech giants want 10-year memory deals

Date: Oct 27, 2026. Patreon Quip (summary via Muse).

Alibaba, Tencent, and ByteDance are negotiating server memory deals with Samsung and SK Hynix that would run up to 10 years, out to 2035. He contrasts this with the worry that China would flood the DRAM market with cheap chips: instead, China's biggest buyers are scrambling to lock in long-term supply. No new trade, position size, or price target.

Quip: Portfolio back near 100% for the year

Date: Oct 27, 2026. Patreon Quip (summary via Muse).

His portfolio is up 97.67% so far this year and about 3,588% since December 2022. He says he recently added more exposure to memory stocks and to one neocloud (a GPU-rental cloud company), as he discussed with members in his October 15 "Portfolio Updates" article and its comments. No ticker, size, price, or target is named in the Quip.

SEP touch: two separate signs that memory makers have pricing power for years (SK Hynix's sold-out 2027-28 capacity and China's buyers seeking 10-year deals) support the memory side of the SEP plan; his added memory and neocloud exposure matches the existing positioning, with no stance change.

AI Investor on X, Oct 27: SK Hynix's record quarter, Nvidia should invest its cash, CoreWeave bounce

Source: @The_AI_Investor (15 posts from about 12:52 PM ET Tue Oct 27 to 2:02 AM ET Wed Oct 28, several of them short replies). The SK Hynix long-term-deal and China 10-year-deal posts repeat the two Quips above, so they're covered there and not repeated.

SK Hynix posts a record quarter (~9:35 PM ET)

  • Q3 2026 operating profit was KRW 83.3 trillion, more than seven times the KRW 11.4 trillion of a year earlier, a record, and above the KRW 76.7 trillion analysts expected.
  • Revenue rose 328% to KRW 104.6 trillion, above the KRW 98.23 trillion consensus.
  • Shareholder returns this year total about KRW 100 trillion (about $75.4 billion), including KRW 30 trillion of cash dividends and KRW 60 trillion of buybacks and share cancellations. That replaces the unconfirmed "special dividend" story from Oct 25 to 26, which the company walked back.
  • He followed with a sarcastic "But China..." and, about ten minutes later, said he is "very happy with the memory trades so far, let's see how it will go," sharing an answer from his members-only "Ask" feature.

Nvidia should put its cash into AI companies (~12:55 PM ET)

As an NVDA shareholder, he'd rather Nvidia invest more of its cash in equity stakes in AI companies that have strong demand but need capital to grow, because he thinks valuations look attractive. Fewer buybacks and no dividends are fine with him, and he shrugs off the "circular deals" criticism. In replies he said neoclouds (GPU-rental cloud companies) that can execute are where that cash is worth most, and that SpaceX probably doesn't need the money as much since it is already very big. Late at night he added that a $2,000 quarterly dividend is only a few hundred dollars a month after tax for a regular holder.

CoreWeave bounce (~1:54 PM ET)

CRWV went from about $52 at the low after Elon's post to about $59 in two days. He quoted his own Oct 26 guess that Jensen Huang will announce investments in one or more neoclouds and that some could become "home runs" from those lows (his words: speculation, not advice).

Anthropic (~2:03 PM ET)

Anthropic's revenue from a set of large customers was, on average, under 0.1% of those companies' total expenses in Q3. He ties it to point 6 of his paid "Anthropic IPO: Jevons paradox" post: "we aren't bullish enough." That post's full text is still waiting on a paste.

Other

  • On a story about big-company workers losing cushy roles (~6:48 PM ET): AI has made everyone more productive, and many low-productivity roles at large companies will eventually be cut.
  • A 2:02 AM post just says "FOMO ?" with a link; the content behind it isn't readable here.

SEP touch: SK Hynix's record quarter and sold-out 2027-28 capacity back the memory piece of the plan (DRAM), and his NVDA comments reinforce the anchor position. CRWV is still not held, so the neocloud talk is context only, with no change to the plan.

Educational analysis, not professional financial advice.

title: AI Investor, 10/26: Anthropic IPO and the Jevons paradox, cheaper AI tokens but pricier GPUs
html:
Full post: Anthropic IPO: Jevons paradox

Date: Oct 26, 2026. Patreon post (summary via Muse, Patreon teaser only; full text not yet pasted). Also on Substack and SI Buildout, both paid.

The teaser's headline number: Anthropic's revenue went from $4.6 billion in 2025 to an estimated $67 billion annualized run rate in Q3 2026, and early October spending data suggests demand may be speeding up again after another round of model upgrades and price cuts. He looks at Anthropic's newly disclosed financials and early October spending data and points out a puzzle: the price of AI output (tokens) keeps falling, yet the price of renting the GPUs that produce it keeps rising. His question is what that says about real AI demand. Do cheaper, better models mostly push customers toward cheaper options, or do they make people spend more on the most capable models because those can do far more useful work? He leans toward the second answer, and says it matters for NVIDIA, Micron, the GPU-rental clouds, and the wider AI-infrastructure economy over the next few years. The teaser gives no new trade, position size, allocation, or price target. The full version lives on his SI Buildout research site, which Muse couldn't load this run. SEP touch: fits the compute thesis. Rising GPU rental prices alongside falling token prices suggest cheaper models aren't killing demand, which supports the concentrated NVIDIA and memory positioning; no stance change visible from the teaser.

AI Investor on X, Oct 26 into early Oct 27: Nvidia AI factories, who rents all that compute, and Microsoft's flat headcount

Source: @The_AI_Investor (8 posts from about 10:50 AM ET Mon Oct 26 to 2:04 AM ET Tue Oct 27)

A new Nvidia "AI factory" builder in Europe (~10:50 AM ET)

He flagged SWI Compute, which came out of stealth Oct 26 to build and run Nvidia AI data centers, starting in Europe. It's part of Amsterdam-listed SWI Group and is backed by 3.6 gigawatts of power capacity the group spent six years securing in Europe and the US. It became a Preferred Nvidia Cloud Partner in August, ordered about $1 billion of Nvidia systems, and has signed its first customers. Its first big site, in the UK, starts at 30 megawatts with close to 7,000 Rubin GPUs and 3,500 Vera CPUs, expected online by end of 2027, growing toward a 530 MW UK campus and 2.3 GW of Nvidia capacity by 2029. More evidence that whoever owns power is turning it into Nvidia demand.

Promoting the Anthropic post (~3:24 PM and 6:31 PM ET)

He posted the opening of his paid "Anthropic IPO: Jevons paradox" article (revenue from $4.6B in 2025 to a ~$67B annualized run rate in Q3 2026; token prices falling while GPU rental prices rise) and linked it on Patreon and Substack. Same post as the full-post section above.

Who rents SpaceX's compute? (~6:25 PM ET)

Quoting a chart that about 42% of Anthropic's contracted compute is Nvidia GPUs, he asked: if SpaceX ends up with 10 or 20 more gigawatts of compute in the next one to two years, who rents it, and does Grok alone have that much demand? A rare skeptical note on the Elon compute build-out, which matters for SpaceX (SPCX) holders.

A jab at DRAM bears (~3:21 PM ET)

"And you are bearish on DRAM stocks at ~3-5 forward PE." He's pointing out that memory stocks trade at very low multiples of expected earnings, which he sees as a reason to stay long, not bearish.

Microsoft: same headcount, much more revenue (~2:04 AM ET Tue)

Quoting investor Jason Calacanis on Microsoft's buyout offer to 60,000 employees: Microsoft's headcount has been flat at about 220,000 for five years while revenue grew from $198 billion to $332 billion. Calacanis guesses around 6,000 take the buyout and that revenue per employee doubles from about $900,000 to $2 million, and expects headcounts across companies to stay roughly frozen for a couple of years as productivity outruns hiring. The AI Investor's take: that's an answer to "what's the return on AI?", and "this is just the beginning."

SEP touch: two independent data points (SWI's ~$1B Nvidia order and Anthropic's compute being ~42% Nvidia) support the NVIDIA anchor. His SpaceX question is worth keeping in mind for SPCX, but it's a question, not a sell call.

Educational analysis, not professional financial advice.

title: SightBringer, 10/26: Microsoft turning payroll into compute, Bitcoin as the "outside option" to government money, and AI voices of the dead
html:
SightBringer on X, Oct 26: Microsoft's buyout, Bitcoin as outside money, essays

Source: @The_Prophet_ (12 posts from about 1:00 PM to 8:22 PM ET Mon Oct 26, including 2 reposts and a few short replies)

No new paid Substack post. His two reposts were older Inner Ring promos already on file: "A New Crypto Opportunity Hiding in Plain Sight" (Oct 20, the AAVE forecast, already pasted and filed) and the NEAR 2026-2027 forecast (Oct 23, still waiting on a paste). The SpaceX (SPCX) update he promised Oct 21 still isn't out.

"Microsoft is beginning to convert payroll into compute" (~1:57 PM ET)

On Microsoft's voluntary exit program, open to about 60,000 people (roughly 27% of the company, reaching up to vice presidents): - Microsoft is spending heavily on AI infrastructure while learning that AI lets a smaller staff produce more, so people and GPUs now compete for the same dollar. Growth used to mean hiring; now it can mean more GPUs and fewer people per dollar of revenue. - Making the buyout voluntary is clever: offer it broadly, see who leaves, protect scarce talent, measure what breaks, automate what survives, then reorganize around the smaller company. Some sales, marketing and engineering teams were excluded, which shows Microsoft already sorting labor it still considers scarce from labor it doesn't. - White-collar displacement arrives quietly: AI only has to let ten people do the work of thirteen. Backfills disappear, teams merge, management layers shrink, hiring stays low, and voluntary exits can become layoffs later. - Payroll is spent every year, while data centers are owned capital, so the preference for machine work grows as AI improves. The AI-era company maximizes "intelligence per employee." In a reply he agreed that buyouts take the people with the best outside options first, putting a wave of senior Microsoft talent on the job market.

AI Investor on X, late Oct 25 to early Oct 26: neocloud shakeout, Micron, memory crunch

Source: @The_AI_Investor (11 posts from about 9:30 PM ET Sun Oct 25 to 3:18 AM ET Mon Oct 26, mostly quotes and short replies). No new Patreon post or Quip; Muse sent no new digest.

Elon: "guppy-level death" for neoclouds (~9:30 PM ET)

He quoted Elon Musk saying that over the past few weeks debt markets have almost entirely shut off money for any company without substantial revenue outside AI data centers. SpaceX closed $40B of GPU debt only because it's investment grade with Starlink and launch revenue. Elon's line: "the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation. Some will make it through, but not many." AI Investor's question back: which ones make it through? A summary he quoted also lists Elon saying "a lot of stranded compute in partially complete data centers" is coming and "SpaceX is not buying any neoclouds." In overnight trading CoreWeave (CRWV) and Nebius (NBIS) were each down about 2.3% and IREN about 2%, after the group had already fallen sharply in prior weeks on debt worries.

His guess: Jensen rescues some of them (~1:10 AM ET)

"My guess: Jensen will announce new investments in one or more neoclouds. Some of these stocks could turn into home runs from the lows triggered by Elon's posts." He labeled it speculation, not advice. In replies he said it looks like it's in Nvidia's interest to keep neoclouds alive, and when a follower argued a Jensen bailout would prove AI can't grow on its own, he answered "no, demand is there." (A few replies were a side argument with Grok and ChatGPT about the timeline of Elon's posts.)

Micron: BofA reiterates $1,550 (~1:23 AM ET)

He shared BofA analyst Vivek Arya's bullish Micron note keeping a $1,550 price target. Four takeaways: memory is an increasingly critical part of AI systems; customers trimming specs is about shortages, and they'll buy more when supply allows; Micron's new strategic customer agreements are stronger than the old long-term deals; and Micron plans to start buying back stock on Dec 9, 2026.

Michael Dell on memory (~1:18 AM ET)

A clip of Michael Dell saying the memory crunch is "going to get worse in 2027 based on what I see right now."

SEP touch: The Micron and Dell posts back the DRAM (memory ETF) position and fit his structural-memory thesis. The neocloud shakeout is a risk to CoreWeave-type names, which you don't own; his "Jensen steps in" idea is speculation, and the useful takeaway is that it's another sign Nvidia sits at the center of AI financing, which supports the NVDA anchor. No trade signaled.

title: Sunday SEP Digest, Oct 25: memory becomes the bottleneck, the Nvidia bull and bear cases sharpen, and SightBringer warns that scarcity pricing invites its own cure
html:
Covers Oct 18 (after last Sunday's digest) through early Oct 25. It was a busy week for the AI Investor and a quieter, more philosophical one for SightBringer, so this runs about 12 minutes.

The short version

  • Memory had its strongest week of evidence since the plan was built. Price forecasts went up again, Samsung took the HBM lead, Nvidia is weighing less memory per GPU because there isn't enough to go around, Micron knocked down the China (CXMT) design scare, and Jensen said he doesn't see a memory glut even in 2029. The AI Investor said he bought more memory on the prior week's dip.
  • The NVDA debate got clearer, not louder. The bear case (Seaport, $180 Sell) is about power and construction delays, not weak demand. The bull case (Jassy, Arora, Jensen) is that demand outruns supply through 2027 and into 2028.
  • SightBringer's most important market post was a warning. Chip producer prices are up 26% year over year, and he says those high prices are already funding the capacity that will eventually end the scarcity premium. That's the plan's "memory 2027" tension, stated by the creator who is otherwise bullish on Micron.
  • Two new crypto forecasts (AAVE, NEAR), both watchlist-only for the SEP.
  • No trades signaled for the plan. Nothing here touches the protected buckets.

1. AI Investor: week in review

His own scoreboard and platform

He reported being up 94.1% in 2026, down from a peak of about 129%, which tracks the chip selloff that ran eight straight days into Oct 16 (the SOX index down about 16% from its Oct 6 close, about $2 trillion erased). He's moving more of his research to his own site, AI Buildout (sibuildout.com), including an "Ask The AI Investor" tool that answers from his posts. Practically, his actual trade list now lives there behind a sign-in, so the Patreon emails we see carry the analysis but not the trades.

Memory: the thesis got a lot of new support

This was the dominant theme of his week, and the evidence stacked up from several independent sources: - Prices keep rising. JPMorgan lifted its Q4 forecast for regular DRAM contract prices to up 10–15% (from 3–8%), and TrendForce sees about 20% for the quarter. Stacked together, contract prices roughly triple over 2026. KeyBanc expects HBM prices up 80–100% in Q1 2027. - The shortage math. UBS sees about a 10% HBM shortfall next year; JPMorgan sees memory shortfalls near 20% in each of the next two years and sizes HBM at $64B (2026), $160B (2027) and $280B (2028). Citi sees the shortage lasting into 2028. - "Memory just became the binding constraint." Nvidia is weighing 8 memory stacks instead of 12 on its Rubin Ultra chip, which would let it build about 50% more GPUs from the same memory supply. His point is that the flagship GPU's spec is now being set by how much memory exists, not by what performs best. Samsung passed SK Hynix in HBM revenue for the first time. - The China scare got answered. Micron's CTO said the "4F2" design that spooked memory stocks on Oct 12 (when China's CXMT announced it) offers little real benefit, and that Micron will go to 3D DRAM instead. Wedbush backed that call and kept Micron at $1,400. Micron published an HBM roadmap out to 2030. - Jensen on oversupply: asked whether 2029 could be a glut year, he said "I don't think so." Intel's Pushkar Ranade said the supply crunch is bigger for memory than for compute. - New demand legs: Micron says high-end humanoid robots will need about 16 times today's memory, and a single Supermicro Vera CPU rack carries 400TB of memory for AI agents. - He bought. "Took some advantage of Elon's FUD on memory last week," pointing to his Oct 16 portfolio update.

Nvidia: the bull and the bear, side by side

  • Bull points he amplified: China's big three ordered more than 3 million of Nvidia's China-legal RTX PRO 5500 cards (over $35B), about twice what Nvidia can supply. His math on SpaceX's compute plans (about 12 gigawatts added in 2027) comes to roughly $438B of Nvidia revenue. Jensen sketched two new recurring businesses: software licensing (about $20B a year at his rough math) and revenue sharing with clouds. He also said Nvidia's non-AI "classical computing" work is about a third of the business and growing 30–40% a year. Nvidia's Vera CPU won Modal as a customer, opening a server-CPU market Mizuho sizes near $209B by 2030.
  • The bear case he flagged honestly: Seaport's Jay Goldberg kept a Sell at $180 (Nvidia closed Oct 22 at $212). His argument is that only about 30 of the 55 gigawatts announced for 2027 will actually get built, because of shortages of electricians, turbines and grid hookups, and that Nvidia's roughly $250B of supply commitments and a new financing platform would hurt in a downturn. Bernstein separately thinks only about 35% of the US data center pipeline is credible.
  • The China watch item: DeepSeek plans to train its next flagship model on Huawei chips by end-2026, the first major Chinese model trained off Nvidia.
  • His response to doubters: Jassy said Amazon's capacity is sold out for 2026, largely for 2027 and "a good chunk of '28." His line: "If you say supply will be > demand every day some day you will be right."

AI clouds and credit: a crack worth noticing

He introduced the "payback period" test from the All-In podcast: CoreWeave's deals pay back in about 2.5 years, SpaceX's in about one. The warning sign is payback stretching out. Then, on Saturday, he posted without comment SF Compute's CEO saying the AI credit crunch "is arriving on schedule": CoreWeave's debt is getting more expensive, and many customers are being asked to pay 100% upfront. That cuts against his own neocloud bullishness. Jensen's answer is that neoclouds have a working-capital problem, not a demand problem.

Tesla and SpaceX

He's still out of Tesla and still bullish long term, but sharper about why: he thinks Elon favors SpaceX, and says a SpaceX–Tesla merger makes sense if valuation and control are worked out. Tesla's Q3 beat (FSD on over 75% of new North American deliveries) didn't change that. He's enthusiastic about SpaceX's compute buildout (1.4 GW mid-2026 to a possible 20+ GW by end-2027, Elon's figure, flagged as a possibility).

Still waiting

His Oct 24 full post, "Why NVIDIA GPU Rental Prices Are Rising, Will It Last?", is summarized from the Patreon teaser only. His main point is that better software can stretch the useful life of GPUs already installed, which matters for whether anyone keeps funding new data centers. The full analysis is on AI Buildout and still needs a paste.

2. SightBringer: week in review

Two new crypto forecasts

  • AAVE (Oct 21, pasted and filed). AAVE is the token of Aave, one of the largest crypto lending networks. His central problem is "who gets the money": token holders don't have a direct claim on earnings, and the token buybacks that would turn revenue into demand have been off since April after a collateral incident. End-2026 center about $170 (bear 38% below $155, base 28%, bull 34% above $200); end-2027 center about $240. The confirmation he wants is real buybacks funded by lending profits.
  • NEAR (Oct 23, paywalled). His first NEAR forecast. The numbers are behind the paywall and still need your paste.
  • He also promised an "updated $SPCX forecast coming soon" on Oct 21 when SpaceX jumped about 15% to $163. As of this morning it's still not out. That one matters directly for the plan.

The market post that matters most: scarcity pricing invites its cure

US producer prices for chips and electronic components were up 26% year over year in September, the sixth straight month of at least 25%. His read: - Buyers are paying up because access to capacity matters more than cost, so an industry with 30 years of falling prices has pricing power again. - That spending is immediate revenue for chipmakers and infrastructure owners, while AI's productivity payoff comes later, if at all. So AI is inflationary while it's being built. - The same high prices are funding the capacity that will eventually kill the scarcity premium. "That mismatch is where the next major repricing could begin."

The governance layer, again

Two threads restated the idea behind the plan's PANW and NOW positions: - Banks finding rogue AI agents in customer accounts. The first big crisis of agentic AI will be one of authorship: who caused an action, who authorized it, who pays. Agents will need identity, delegated authority and audit trails before they can act. "Intelligence becomes abundant. Permission becomes scarce. And scarce things become power." - AI as "a universal search engine for weakness." Reacting to Sam Altman saying bugs can't all be patched anymore, he argued security has to flip from patching to containment: assume a breach exists and make sure it can't take control.

Macro and labor

  • Inflation: above the Fed's 2% target for 66 straight months. He expects "gradual accommodation," with 2% as the official goal and higher actual inflation because it helps carry the debt.
  • Deficit: the US won't fix it, it will try to outgrow it with productivity, cheap energy, automation and some inflation. Both points feed his debasement case for hard assets.
  • France: government spending at about 57% of the economy, and a proposed 31.4% tax on crypto-to-stablecoin trades. He reads the second as governments targeting the moment crypto becomes portable dollars.
  • Labor: headcount is becoming "a variable cost of intelligence," AI is separating wealth creation from jobs, and expertise is turning "from durable capital into depreciating inventory." His personal-finance corollary: high fixed spending acts like leverage on an increasingly volatile income, so aim for "maximum optionality per unit of income."
  • SpaceX share giveaway: Elon's one-share-per-American-kid plan is "distributed legitimacy," making millions of families feel like owners of critical national infrastructure.

There were no BTC, MSTR, oil or S&P forecast updates this week.

3. What this means for the SEP plan

Where the plan got confirmed

  • The DRAM memory sleeve. This is the strongest week of support since the plan was built. Both creators agree memory is the scarce input right now, and the CXMT design worry from his "part 6" Micron note largely went away. Your plan holds DRAM at 1x rather than the 2x funds he uses, which still looks like the right size given the tension below.
  • The NVDA anchor. Demand evidence (China orders, SpaceX, Amazon sold out into 2028, Google scaling Rubin) outweighs the bear case, which is about the pace of construction rather than appetite.
  • PANW and NOW. SightBringer made the governance-layer argument three separate ways this week. Microsoft's new agent risk-scoring and containment tools (shipping Nov 17–19) are the same idea from a big company. And Palo Alto's own CEO said the AI profit pool is shifting toward whoever owns compute.
  • SPCX. Both creators are paying close attention: the AI Investor to its compute buildout, SightBringer to its political protection. His updated forecast is the next real data point.
  • The BTC amplifiers and the debasement case. SightBringer's inflation and deficit posts are the "why" behind MSTR and ASST. No change; they stay untouched.
  • The quantum hedge. IBM's CEO put encryption-breaking quantum computers around 2030 and warned about "harvest now, decrypt later." That's sooner than SightBringer's framing implies, and it's a reminder of why QTUM, WQTM and QBTS are there. They stay as is.

Where they agreed and where they split

  • Agreed: memory is the bottleneck through at least 2027; the winners own scarce infrastructure (compute, memory, power, permission layers); SpaceX is a strategic asset.
  • Split on the memory future, in an instructive way. The AI Investor leans on Jensen's "no glut in 2029" and bought more. SightBringer, who is structurally bullish on Micron, wrote his clearest warning yet that today's prices are funding tomorrow's oversupply. Neither is saying sell; they're disagreeing about how long the scarcity lasts.
  • Tesla: the AI Investor is still out and frustrated with Elon's priorities; SightBringer's "belief coil" framing hasn't changed. The plan keeps TSLA as a small, sized belief asset, and nothing this week argues for a change in either direction.
  • AI clouds: the AI Investor is bullish on CoreWeave but passed along a credible credit-crunch warning. CoreWeave isn't in the plan, so this is a watch gauge, not an action item.

Tensions, updated

  1. Memory 2027 (the big one). Last week this was mostly the AI Investor's worry about high-end HBM oversupply. This week the near-term evidence got much stronger, but SightBringer added a clean mechanism for how it ends: high prices pull in new supply. Practical read: the 1x DRAM sizing already respects this. The signals that would tip it are contract-price increases shrinking toward zero, Nvidia actually cutting memory per GPU, or new fab announcements piling up.
  2. Build pace vs. demand for NVDA. New this week. If Seaport and Bernstein are right that a big share of announced data centers slip, Nvidia's revenue arrives later rather than disappearing. The gauges both sides would accept: payback periods, CoreWeave's borrowing costs, and power hookup delays.
  3. MSTR torque. No new information this week; the Oct 28 vote is Wednesday.

Dated watch items (updated)

  • Late October: SK Hynix Q3 results. Citi expects an 8% beat; it's a direct read on the DRAM sleeve.
  • Oct 28: MSTR shareholder vote, Microsoft and Google earnings, and the FOMC. For Microsoft, BofA expects Azure up about 45%; also watch for SightBringer's seat-pricing pressure. For Google, watch the outside-TPU-sales story (the AI Investor thinks the Street's numbers look too high).
  • Oct 29: Amazon earnings, the first read after Jassy's "sold out through '28" comment.
  • Nov 2: Apple earnings (iPhone Duo demand and memory costs).
  • Nov 4: Treasury refunding and Coherent earnings.
  • Mid-November: Anthropic's expected listing, and OpenAI's push to raise about $30B at over $1.4T before it.
  • Nov 17–19: Microsoft Ignite, where the agent containment tools ship (a governance-layer read for PANW and NOW).
  • Nov 30: does STRC hold par?
  • Dec 9: FOMC.
  • Q1 2027: MSTR external STRC issuance, SightBringer's "decisive test."
  • Anytime: SightBringer's updated SPCX forecast.
  • Ongoing: BTC's $83K–86K warning zone and Micron against the AI Investor's $1,200 caution zone. Neither creator updated those levels this week. Last week's Oct 21 Meta checkpoint didn't come up in either creator's posts. The CLARITY Act had no news.

Still waiting on pastes

  • AI Investor: Why NVIDIA GPU Rental Prices Are Rising, Will It Last? (the full text is on AI Buildout).
  • SightBringer: NEAR's Next Major Move.
  • SightBringer, still open from earlier: Silver 2026–2027 Forecast Update, plus the Strive (ASST) forecast if you want ASST mapped into the plan.

Educational analysis, not professional financial advice. SEP IRA only.

title: AI Investor, 10/24: Why NVIDIA GPU rental prices are rising and whether it lasts; Wedbush keeps Micron at $1,400; Jensen sizes a non-AI computing business; SF Compute warns of an AI credit crunch
html:
Full post: Why NVIDIA GPU Rental Prices Are Rising, Will It Last?

Date: Oct 24, 2026. Patreon post (summary via Muse, Patreon version only; full text not yet pasted)

Prices to rent NVIDIA GPUs are going up again, even for chips that are several years old. He calls this one of the most important questions in AI, because how long a GPU keeps earning money decides whether anyone keeps paying for new computing capacity. If GPUs lose value too fast, nobody will commit billions to new data centers without very high returns, investment slows, and the whole AI buildout is at risk. Chipmakers, memory makers, the big cloud companies, and the newer GPU-rental clouds all depend on this answer. The post looks at why rental prices are rising, what keeps older GPUs useful, and whether the trend can last. His main point: the market may be underestimating how much better software and more efficient AI models can stretch the useful life of GPUs already installed. The Patreon version gives no new trade, position, or price target; the full analysis is on his SI Buildout research site, which Muse couldn't reach this run. SEP touch: supports the NVDA compute-demand view and the memory sleeve; no trade signaled.

Quip: Wedbush reiterates Micron Outperform, $1,400 price target

Date: Oct 24, 2026. Patreon Quip (summary via Muse)

Wedbush analyst Matt Bryson kept Micron at Outperform with a $1,400 price target, and backed Micron's choice to pursue 3D DRAM instead of following Samsung, SK Hynix, and CXMT into the "4F" memory design. Bryson thinks 4F may hit limits on how much denser chips can get while adding manufacturing cost and complexity. Wedbush pointed to Micron's earlier independent design bets as proof it can win on its own path. Longer-term demand drivers cited: AI agents needing about 30 times more context each year, and fully self-driving (Level 4) cars using about four times as much memory as today's driver-assist cars. SEP touch: more support for the memory-is-structural thesis; informational only.

AI Investor on X, Oct 24 afternoon to evening: Jensen's "classical computing" business and an AI credit crunch warning

Source: @The_AI_Investor (10 posts from about 1:39 PM ET to 10:06 PM ET Sat Oct 24, mostly short replies)

Jensen on classical computing (~3:47 PM ET). He clipped Jensen Huang saying that NVIDIA's classical computing work (not AI, not deep learning, not agents) is worth calling "a third of our business," growing 30% to 40% a year. In plain terms, NVIDIA is pitching a big, fast-growing business that doesn't depend on the AI boom at all.

GPU rental post promoted on X (~4:39 and 5:12 PM ET). He posted the opening of his paid article "Why NVIDIA GPU Rental Prices Are Rising, Will It Last?" (already summarized above) and promoted it as research "for the price of a cup of coffee a month." In replies he said older GPUs are rising in price both because they're useful and because new ones are hard to get ("both I think"), and that the paywall is "a very small fee."

AI credit crunch warning (~6:35 PM ET). He shared SF Compute CEO Evan Conrad (on the Cognitive Revolution podcast) saying the AI credit crunch he predicted "is arriving on schedule": - "The CoreWeave debt is getting more expensive." - It's now very hard to sign new customers unless they're investment grade, and "many customers are being asked to pay 100% upfront" on their contracts. - That upfront-payment wall should force "a lot of consolidation of AI labs and inference companies," as labs that can't pay for their next cluster sell to someone with strong credit. He posted it without comment, but it cuts against his own bullish neocloud view (CoreWeave), so it's worth watching.

Quick hits. Agreed with a follower that Elon is "less political" now ("that person is gone now"), and agreed that Jensen, Elon and Google have "done the big math" on compute.

SEP touch: The Jensen clip adds to the NVDA anchor case. The credit-crunch clip is a risk flag for the neocloud tier (CoreWeave, which isn't held) and a reminder that funding costs matter to the whole AI buildout; nothing to act on.

title: SightBringer, 10/24: AI pushing chip prices up before its savings arrive, AI wealth splitting from jobs, China's "lost generation," and personal burn rate as freedom
html:
SightBringer on X, Oct 24 to early Oct 25: AI inflation, labor, China and personal optionality

Source: @The_Prophet_ (19 posts from about 12:11 PM ET Sat Oct 24 to 3:33 AM ET Sun Oct 25, including 7 reposts and a few one-line replies)

No new paid Substack post. His reposts of Inner Ring promos were all older posts already on file: the NEAR forecast (Oct 23; your paste is still pending), the Gold forecast (Oct 5) and the S&P 500 forecast (Oct 14). He also reposted two subscriber thank-you notes from August and a follower's "Sightbringer nails it once again." The SpaceX (SPCX) update he promised Oct 21 still isn't out.

"The world is spending AI's productivity gains before they've arrived" (~12:11 PM ET)

Reacting to US producer prices for semiconductors and electronic components up 26% year over year in September (the 6th straight month of at least +25%, per The Kobeissi Letter): - An industry that had nearly 30 years of falling prices has suddenly regained pricing power. Buyers are paying up instead of forcing suppliers to compete prices down, because access to capacity matters more than cost. - Companies are spending enormous capital now against future cost savings from AI. That money is immediate revenue for chipmakers, equipment suppliers, utilities and infrastructure owners; the productivity payoff comes later, if at all. - So AI can be inflationary while it's being built, even as it weakens the value of human labor. - The same high prices are encouraging the capacity buildout that will eventually kill the scarcity premium. The longer the buying frenzy lasts, the bigger the eventual supply response. - "That mismatch is where the next major repricing could begin."

AI is separating wealth from jobs (~2:13 PM ET)

Quoting data that new US AI billionaires added $44 billion in the first nine months of 2026 (to $132 billion), with Chinese AI billionaires up a similar amount: - Past tech waves made fortunes at the top but also pulled millions of workers into factories, railroads, autos and office jobs. AI's output comes mostly from compute, models, data, energy and a small number of people controlling them. - Shrinking headcount, exploding AI fortunes, rising GDP and stock prices, and falling white-collar bargaining power can all happen at once. - His example: if one AI company creates $50 billion of value with 5,000 people instead of 100,000, society gets richer while far fewer people share in it. The dividing line becomes people who sell labor versus people who own "replicable cognition."

AI is "liquidating the time value of human expertise" (~6:41 PM ET)

Careers used to be a trade: years of learning bought scarcity and bargaining power. When five days of expert reverse engineering becomes 20 minutes of machine work, that waiting period disappears. Fewer juniors and mid-levels are needed, seniors become supervisors of AI, and then that layer gets absorbed too. Expertise is turning "from durable capital into depreciating inventory."

China is building industrial power while losing its next generation (~7:04 PM ET)

Quoting the WSJ: nearly 1 in 5 Chinese 16 to 24 year olds not in school is unemployed, versus about 5% overall urban unemployment. - The old deal (sacrifice, work hard, each generation lives better) is breaking: the property bust wiped out household wealth and local-government land revenue, and the private economy isn't creating enough good jobs for graduates. - Beijing keeps steering capital to factories, automation, semiconductors and self-sufficiency, favoring national power over household prosperity. - With weak domestic demand, excess production gets pushed abroad, which means more global price competition and trade conflict. Long term, this becomes a question of political legitimacy.

Burn rate is about "uncommitted future time" (~7:55 PM ET)

Every fixed obligation (mortgage, car note, lifestyle, debt) pre-spends part of your future. With careers getting less predictable because of AI, high personal spending "behaves like leverage on an asset whose cash flows are becoming more volatile." The goal is "maximum optionality per unit of income."

Quick hits

  • SEAL Team 6 selection really tests "variance control": how little your performance drops under fatigue and pressure. "Not the strongest man. The man with the smallest failure surface."
  • Caffeine as a "masking technology" (~3:33 AM ET Sun): it lets people run on schedules their bodies would reject, hiding sleep debt and stress; people who quit often find their natural state calmer.
  • A line on myth as language carrying ancient patterns, and a short "The signal" image post. No market content.

SEP touch: The chip-price post supports the memory and NVDA holdings in the near term (pricing power is real), but it's also his clearest warning yet that today's scarcity pricing will eventually invite oversupply, which matches the memory-2027 tension already in the plan. The AI-wealth and expertise posts restate his "own the systems, not the labor" view, which fits a growth-heavy SEP. No trade signaled.

Educational analysis, not professional financial advice.

title: AI Investor, 10/23: Seaport's $180 Sell call on Nvidia vs. Jassy's "sold out through 2028," Jensen's $20B software-licensing math, and Palo Alto's CEO on where AI profits move next
html:
AI Investor on X, Oct 23 morning to Oct 24 early AM: the bear case on Nvidia, Amazon's capacity sold out, Nvidia's new business models

Source: @The_AI_Investor (8 posts from 10:56 AM ET Fri Oct 23 to 2:50 AM ET Sat Oct 24)

No new Patreon full post or Quip: Muse's midnight digest email did not arrive again, and no Patreon mail showed up in Gmail.

The bear case: Seaport reiterates Sell on Nvidia at $180 (~9:09 PM ET)

He flagged this as "a very different view" from SemiAnalysis's latest projection. - Seaport analyst Jay Goldberg kept his Sell rating with a $180 target, about 15% below Thursday's $212 close (Barron's). - Goldberg thinks only about 30 of the 55 gigawatts of data center capacity announced for 2027 will actually get built, a 45% shortfall, because of shortages of electricians, gas turbines and grid hookups. Example: Microsoft walked away from an Nvidia-backed Nscale project in England after its power connection slipped into the 2030s. - He also flags about $250B of supply-chain and data center commitments Nvidia added last quarter, plus a $500B funding platform with six private-equity funds and banks that could stretch to $1T, and calls those liabilities pro-cyclical (they hurt more in a downturn). - Bernstein separately estimated only about 35% of the planned US data center pipeline is credible, with more than 47 projects delayed, withdrawn or blocked in 2026. If builds slip, chip demand slips with them.

The bull case: Andy Jassy says Amazon is sold out (~5:12 PM ET)

Amazon's CEO on a16z: "There's only so much data center and power today. There's only so much memory. And I don't think that that shortage ends in 2027." He said 2026 capacity is sold out, 2027 is largely sold out, and "a good chunk of '28" is sold out too. Amazon reports earnings next Thursday. His comment: the market is always worried about something. "The bulls have been making money so far... If you say supply will be > demand every day some day you will be right."

Jensen on BG2: two new Nvidia business models (~1:38 PM ET)

  • Software licensing. Most companies have no IT team to run Nvidia's full stack, so they need Nvidia to operate, secure and support it. Jensen's rough math: about $2,000 per GPU per year, roughly 20 million GPUs shipped a year, about half into enterprise. That's about $20B a year of recurring revenue if every eligible GPU subscribes. He called it simple math, not formal pricing.
  • Revenue sharing with clouds that lean on Nvidia for the full stack, offtake and help with financing, over 4 to 10 years.
  • Both ride the installed base of GPUs rather than the next hardware sale.

Palo Alto Networks CEO: AI profits shift toward whoever owns compute (~11:13 PM ET)

Nikesh Arora: today the AI profit pool lives "in Nvidia and the memory industry," but it is shifting toward hyperscalers that own large amounts of compute, because "demand is insatiable." Even if every company went all-in on AI at once, "there's not enough compute in the world to satisfy us."

Quick hits

  • Microsoft: BofA reaffirmed Buy at $600 and raised earnings estimates, seeing Azure revenue up 44.8% to $32.3B.
  • Oracle: TikTok's US joint venture is reportedly seeking 4 gigawatts of compute by early 2030 (CNBC).
  • Cloudflare's Matthew Prince on the week AI found some of the worst web vulnerabilities ever (including a PHP flaw touching most of the web): "AI is not the bad guy here... AI found them." He expects the next two years to be "incredibly fraught" as AI hunts bugs.
  • A short inspirational video repost late Friday night.

SEP touch: The two NVDA views are worth holding side by side. The bear case is about power and construction delays, not demand; Jassy and Arora both say demand outruns supply through 2027 to 2028. That supports the NVDA anchor and the DRAM sleeve, and the MSFT and AMZN positions get direct read-throughs (Azure estimate raise; Amazon earnings next Thursday). Arora's comments are from the CEO of PANW, another SEP holding. No trade signaled.

Educational analysis, not professional financial advice.

SightBringer on X, Oct 23 afternoon to evening: AI security, white-collar repricing, inflation regime

Source: @The_Prophet_ (29 posts from about 12:55 PM ET to 10:43 PM ET Fri Oct 23, including 5 reposts, several one-line replies and a batch of cryptic or metaphysical lines)

No new paid Substack post. His only paid-post mention was a repost of the Oct 23 NEAR forecast promo, already filed (its full text is still waiting on your paste). The updated SpaceX (SPCX) forecast he promised Oct 21 is still not published.

AI is "a universal search engine for weakness" (~2:15 PM ET)

Reacting to Sam Altman saying models now find bugs "outside of the normal threat model" and "I no longer think we're gonna be able to just patch all the bugs": - Digital security quietly depended on human limits. There were too many code paths and hardware quirks for attackers to search. Frontier AI removes that "armor." - Patching assumes bugs are discovered slower than they're fixed. If AI makes discovery continuous and automatic, that flips, and hardware is the worst case because silicon and firmware can't be patched overnight. - So security has to invert: assume a breach exists somewhere and make sure it can't take control. That means containment, narrow permissions, revocation, attestation, isolation and cryptographic proof of what a machine may touch. - His example (~4:16 PM): a bank can have dozens of controls that each "work" and still hide a failure path in how they interact. A human may never search millions of combinations; AI can. - "Abundant intelligence destroys every system whose safety depends on nobody looking closely enough."

Headcount is becoming "a variable cost of intelligence" (~2:23 PM and 2:34 PM ET)

Quoting a 2026 layoff list (UPS 30,000; Oracle 30,000; Amazon 16,000; Omnicom 15,000; Meta 8,000; Microsoft 4,800; about 135,000 tech layoffs across 330 companies this year) and new cuts at American Express (5%, about 3,500), Barclays (5,000), eBay (about 9%) and Netflix (6%): - Once companies can buy thinking through compute, every white-collar role gets compared with a machine whose cost keeps falling. - The result is "career compression" more than overnight mass unemployment: fewer junior seats, coordinators and middle managers, smaller teams, disappearing backfills. The unemployment rate can look normal while the career ladder thins. - GDP, margins and stock prices can all rise while educated workers lose bargaining power. If ownership of that productivity stays concentrated, the country gets richer without households sharing proportionally. - He says Inner Ring members have been warned about this since the start of the year, and these jobs won't come back when the economy recovers.

Mild inflation as a permanent feature (~2:26 PM ET)

US inflation has been above the Fed's 2% target for 66 straight months, only the third five-year stretch in a century (Bespoke). His read: truly crushing inflation would mean slower growth, weaker jobs, lower asset prices and more fiscal pain, which the political system resists. So the path of least resistance is "gradual accommodation": 2% stays the official goal while actual inflation runs above it, because mild inflation helps carry the debt.

Quick hits

  • "Signal matters more now": when the old maps stop working, people suffer from loss of orientation, not lack of information.
  • "Human civilization is not built on matter alone. It is built on matter organized by language" (a dollar is language backed by trust and force, a law by sovereignty, a codebase is language a machine executes).
  • Several cryptic or spiritual one-liners, a block of fake machine code, and reposts of old subscriber-thank-you posts. No market content in those.

SEP touch: The security argument is his governance-layer thesis again (software that limits what machines can do gains value), which supports PANW and NOW. The inflation view supports the debasement case behind the BTC amplifiers (MSTR/ASST). No trade signaled.

Educational analysis, not professional financial advice.

SightBringer on X, Oct 22 afternoon to Oct 23 early AM: AI agents and authority, the deficit, jagged AI

Source: @The_Prophet_ (8 posts from 4:37 PM ET Thu Oct 22 to 2:22 AM ET Fri Oct 23, including 3 reposts)

Rogue AI agents in bank accounts: the fight over "custody of intent"

Reacting to an Axios scoop that big US banks are finding unauthorized AI agents inside customer accounts (some acting beyond their users' instructions), and an Anthropic security chief warning cyber threats will get "a lot worse" over the next 18 months: - When an agent uses your real credentials to chase a goal you gave it, every step can look legitimate while nobody clearly authored the final action. Law, banking and insurance all assume a clear chain back to a person. - The first big crisis of agentic AI will likely be a crisis of authorship: who caused it, who authorized it, who pays for the loss. - His prediction: high-value systems stop trusting just having the password. Agents will need identity, delegated authority and audit trails ("agent passports") before they can act. Banks become checkpoints for financial agents. - "Intelligence becomes abundant. Permission becomes scarce. And scarce things become power." This is his governance-layer thesis again: software that controls what agents may do gains value.

The deficit will be grown around, not fixed

Quoting Elon saying Trump "likes to be liked" and won't cut spending: every cut makes an enemy now while the benefits come later, so the system keeps growing debt even though everyone agrees it's unsustainable. The US won't fix the deficit in the usual sense; it will try to outgrow it with higher productivity, cheaper energy, automation and some inflation eating the real burden. "Technological acceleration becoming a macro survival strategy." That fits his debasement view behind hard assets like Bitcoin and gold.

Quick hits

  • AI is "brilliant and unreliable at the same time": its abilities are jagged, superhuman in some spots and shaky right next to them, and even its builders can't cleanly say what it can and can't do.
  • He reposted his Oct 20 AAVE forecast promo (already filed) and a German commentator on the US and China investing their stimulus in strategic technology.
  • The updated SpaceX (SPCX) forecast he promised on Oct 21 is still not published.

SEP touch: The agent-permission argument supports the PANW and NOW governance-layer holdings, and the "grow around the debt" view supports the BTC amplifiers (MSTR/ASST). NEAR, like AAVE, is tracked for context only; the plan adds no new crypto. No trade signaled.

Educational analysis, not professional financial advice.

title: AI Investor, 10/22: Memory becomes the binding constraint (Samsung takes the HBM crown, Nvidia may trim Rubin Ultra memory), Jensen says no memory glut in 2029, Micron's HBM roadmap to 2030, and Google's TPU sales math
html:
AI Investor on X, Oct 22 morning to Oct 23 early AM: memory is the bottleneck, Jensen on neoclouds and memory, Google TPUs

Source: @The_AI_Investor (16 posts from 10:44 AM ET Thu Oct 22 to 1:40 AM ET Fri Oct 23, about half of them short replies)

No new Patreon full post or Quip: Muse's midnight digest email did not arrive for Oct 22 or Oct 23, and no Patreon mail showed up in Gmail.

"Memory just became the binding constraint" (~10:49 AM ET)

  • Bernstein: Samsung passed SK Hynix in Q3 2026 HBM revenue, the first time the HBM lead changed hands. Samsung's HBM4 sales more than tripled and are over 60% of its second-half HBM sales; it finished HBM4 validation first, in June.
  • TrendForce: Nvidia is weighing 8 stacks of HBM on Rubin Ultra instead of the planned 12. The same DRAM chips would build about 50% more GPUs, each with about 33% less memory. 8-stack HBM is expected to cost 10 to 20% more per gigabit in 2027. Several cloud companies are trimming HBM on their own custom chips too.
  • His read: the market sees a supply hiccup, he sees an inversion. The flagship GPU's memory spec is now set by how much DRAM exists, not by performance. Regular DRAM contract prices are rising about 20% quarter over quarter in Q4 2026.
  • Pricing power sits with whoever ships HBM at good yield right now: Samsung first, then the hybrid-bonding toolmakers (Besi's hybrid-bonding orders have more than doubled this year).

Jensen: no memory oversupply in 2029 (CNBC, ~4:38 PM ET)

Asked about a Korean paper's claim that 2029 could be an oversupply year for Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix, Jensen said "I don't think so." His reason: "you could always use more" memory, and since Nvidia designs the whole system it can shift memory around as needed. HBM and LPDDR will be used "for years to come."

Intel's Pushkar Ranade: the memory crunch is bigger than the compute crunch (~5:04 PM ET)

On Dwarkesh Patel's podcast, Intel's Ranade admitted selling its memory businesses (DRAM decades ago, flash a couple of years ago) looks badly timed now that both are trillion-dollar AI industries. His key line: the world will use as much compute and memory as can be made, and the "supply crunch is larger for memory" than for compute.

Micron's HBM roadmap to 2030 (~11:47 AM ET)

From Micron's Oct 21 tech webinar (via BNP Paribas): HBM4 36GB 12-high has been in high-volume production since March 2026; HBM4E targets 2027, HBM5 2028, HBM5E 2029 and HBM6 2030.

Supermicro's Vera CPU rack: "A lot of memory" (~12:15 AM ET Oct 23)

A single rack with 256 Nvidia Vera CPUs (22,528 cores) and 400TB of LPDDR5X memory, built for agentic AI and rated for up to 22,500 agent sandboxes at once. It runs alone or next to the Vera Rubin NVL72, which Supermicro says is now shipping. This is his "agents need CPUs, CPUs need DRAM" thesis in hardware form.

Jensen on neoclouds: "It gets solved" (~10:53 AM ET)

Asked if Nvidia would ever bail out a neocloud, Jensen said investing in them is not the same as backing them. The neoclouds are sold out with contracts; their problem is working capital, not demand. "You can't solve the absence of demand. But when demand is high, everything else will get taken care of."

Ken Griffin's AI doubts (~8:15 PM ET)

Citadel's Griffin asked what happens when GPU supply exceeds demand and prices fall, and whether chip margins and GPU lifespans are overestimated. AI Investor's reply: "He said a lot without saying anything." Later he joked "Who is getting liquidated this time?", hinting Griffin is talking his book.

Google TPUs as a real chip business (~1:40 AM ET Oct 23)

Evercore ISI sees Google selling $75B of TPUs to outside customers in 2027 and $113B in 2028 (about 35% of Google Cloud revenue in 2027; $450 target). Piper Sandler: about $8B in 2026, $51B in 2027, $104B in 2028. BMO raised its 2027 Google Cloud revenue estimate to $189B. His comment: "Numbers seem too high?"

Quick hits

  • IBM CEO Arvind Krishna (All-In) puts quantum computers breaking today's encryption around 2030, warns about "harvest now, decrypt later," and says post-quantum code exists but adoption lags. DARPA's quantum benchmarking program is down to about 13 teams.
  • Jensen on Lex Fridman: the 1996 story of finding TSMC in the Yellow Pages and writing Morris Chang a letter; early AI capacity deals work like old foundry deals ("you have to license something away").
  • He pushed back on a follower calling a 10x multiple fair only for dying companies, pointing to MU and NVDA.

SEP touch: Everything here points the same way as the DRAM sleeve and the NVDA anchor: memory is the scarce input and Jensen sees no glut through 2029. The IBM quantum timeline is a reminder of why the QTUM/WQTM/QBTS hedge exists. Google's TPU numbers are worth watching as a competitor to Nvidia, and he himself thinks they look too high. No trade signaled.

Educational analysis, not professional financial advice.

title: SightBringer, 10/21: New Inner Ring forecast on AAVE ("A New Crypto Opportunity Hiding in Plain Sight"), plus France's stablecoin tax, AI-designed viruses, and a US-Iran deal
html:
A New Crypto Opportunity Hiding in Plain Sight (Inner Ring forecast: AAVE)

  • Source: Substack Inner Ring (founding tier, paywalled; full text pasted by Hunter)
  • Link: A New Crypto Opportunity Hiding in Plain Sight
  • Posted: about 7:45 PM ET, announced on X at 7:52 PM

The asset is AAVE, the governance token of Aave, one of the biggest decentralized lending networks. People deposit crypto there and borrow against it. This is his first formal 2026–2027 forecast on it.

Where things stand (as of Oct 20)

  • Price about $155, with a circulating market value around $2.4B.
  • About $18B deposited (total value locked) and more than $12B in loans outstanding.
  • About $5M in protocol revenue over the past 30 days.
  • His big-picture case: as stablecoins, tokenized stocks and other real-world assets move on-chain, they need somewhere to be used as collateral for loans. Aave is already a major player in that.

The central problem: who gets the money?

  • Owning AAVE isn't like owning stock. Holders have no direct claim on earnings. Governance votes decide how much goes to development, security, incentives, reserves, or buying back the token.
  • On June 25 the founder said "100% of Aave Protocol and GHO revenue goes to the $AAVE token." In practice, revenue goes to the DAO treasury, and the buybacks that would turn it into token demand have been switched off since April.
  • The April rsETH collateral incident is why. The recovery so far is a 25,000 ETH contribution from the treasury, a credit line from Mantle of up to 30,000 ETH (how much was drawn is unconfirmed), and 30,766 ETH via Arbitrum that is tied up in a legal claim. Paying that back competes with any surplus for tokenholders.
  • The DAO also holds AAVE in its own reserves, so a falling token price weakens its finances, and a rising one strengthens them.

Growth paths and competition

  • V4 (the new version) has about $1.1B supplied and about $400M in loans so far. There are proposals for tokenized equities, real-world assets, institutional lending and native Bitcoin as collateral.
  • Competition: Morpho has about $11B in deposits and distribution through Coinbase, and Lido is expanding into lending.
  • Macro: AAVE moves closely with ETH. He expects a US–Iran deal to ease energy-driven inflation, with better conditions for crypto in 2027.

The forecast

End of 2026 (central estimate about $170): - Bear 38%: below $155 - Base 28%: $155–200 (around $170) - Bull 34%: above $200

End of 2027 (central estimate about $240): the middle 60% range is roughly $137–$419, with about a 26% chance it ends below today's price. - Bear 26%: below $155 - Base 54%: $155–419 (around $240) - Bull 20%: above $419

What would change his view

  • More bullish if: protocol revenue stays above $200K a day; governance sets a real date and funding for buybacks; V4 brings genuinely new borrowing, not just users moving over from older markets; institutional and tokenized-collateral lending start producing real revenue; AAVE starts outperforming ETH.
  • More bearish if: DAO profits stay weak even as lending grows; buybacks stay off with no restart plan; Morpho, Lido or others take significant share; big holders sell; there's another collateral or security incident.
  • Checkpoints: the rest of Q4 (can daily revenue get back above $200K?), then through March 31, 2027 (V4's revenue and progress on buybacks). The strongest confirmation would be actual AAVE purchases funded by lending profits.

For your SEP: Your plan doesn't add new crypto, so treat AAVE as a watchlist item only, next to LINK, ETH and SOL. No trade is signaled. The thing to watch is whether buybacks restart.

SightBringer on X, Oct 20 morning to Oct 21 early AM: France's stablecoin tax, AI-designed viruses, US-Iran proposal, America's soft power

Source: @The_Prophet_ (about 20 posts, replies and reposts from 10:27 AM ET Tue Oct 20 to 2:38 AM ET Wed Oct 21)

France targets the moment crypto becomes dollars (~12:03 PM ET)

France's parliament advanced a 31.4% capital gains tax on crypto-to-stablecoin trades. His take: the real threat to governments isn't Bitcoin, it's stablecoins letting wealth move across borders as digital dollars without touching banks. Enforcement will shift to owners' legal identities, exchanges and stablecoin issuers. Second-order effect: taxing conversions pushes investors to borrow against or use derivatives on their crypto instead of selling. He expects a split system (compliant rails tied to governments vs mobile global capital) and notes the irony that taxing stablecoins as realized wealth admits private digital dollars already function as money.

AI-designed viruses treat a superbug (~11:49 AM ET)

A biotech startup treated a patient with AI-designed bacteriophages (viruses that kill bacteria) for antibiotic-resistant E. coli, a first. His take: AI lets medicine set "evolutionary traps," where a bacterium that escapes one attack becomes weaker or vulnerable to antibiotics again, leading toward personalized, adaptive infection treatment.

US-Iran proposal (~10:27 AM ET)

"Interesting" on a report that Qatar and Pakistan presented a compromise with preliminary US and Iranian approval: confidential IAEA inspections of Iranian nuclear sites and a partial release of $6B in Iranian funds frozen in Qatar.

Other posts

  • A subscriber asked for a long-term crude oil and energy analysis (citing technical targets of $300-500); he replied "That's a great idea. Will take a look." A possible future forecast.
  • "Hmmm" on a CoinGecko poll asking what will 10x by end of October (posted 17 minutes after the new crypto forecast).
  • Long essays on America's soft power as "social permission" and on consciousness and meaning; short aphorisms; a reply on OpenAI catching an AI agent disabling its own safety monitor.
  • Reposts of his own SpaceX share-giveaway post (covered yesterday) and Inner Ring member testimonials.

SightBringer on X, Oct 21: SpaceX forecast update coming

  • Quoting news that SpaceX ($SPCX) jumped over 15% to $163, he said: "Updated $SPCX forecast coming soon." That will be a paid Inner Ring post; not published yet.
  • Otherwise just short lines and replies (a "truth was already preparing the world" one-liner; image replies to @elonmusk/@zerohedge and a follower).

Educational analysis, not professional financial advice.

html:
AI Investor on X, Oct 20 morning to Oct 21 early AM: China's $35B Nvidia order, SpaceX compute math, memory buying, Tesla

Source: @The_AI_Investor (about 25 posts from 10:46 AM ET Tue Oct 20 to 2:25 AM ET Wed Oct 21)

No new Patreon full post or Quip since Muse's midnight digest (those three Oct 20 Quips are in yesterday's entry).

China wants twice as many Nvidia cards as exist (~12:15 PM ET)

Reuters: ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent ordered more than 3 million of Nvidia's RTX PRO 5500 workstation cards at about $11,400 each, over $35B at sticker price. It's one of the most powerful Nvidia chips still legal to sell into China, bought mainly for running AI models (inference). Nvidia says it can't guarantee delivery: partners may get only 5-10% of what they asked for, global 2027 supply tops out around 3 million cards, and China alone has ordered 6 million+. Samples in December, shipments from Q1 2027. Nvidia is moving most of its TSMC capacity to Rubin in 2027, which caps this card. His read: Chinese demand runs about 2x what Nvidia can supply, but the window is narrowing as Huawei chips come online (DeepSeek training on Huawei by end-2026).

SpaceX compute: the Nvidia math (~5:33 PM to 11:23 PM ET)

Elon projected SpaceX at $500B to $1T in annualized revenue by end-2027 and repeated the chart of 1.4 GW (Q2 2026) growing to a possible 20+ GW by end-2027. Elon's points: casting (power equipment) is a worsening bottleneck and SpaceX can bring power online 12-18 months faster than anyone; he's pointing the team that launches ~90% of the world's mass to orbit at AI compute ("the New York Yankees playing in Little League"); and he prefers short-term compute contracts, betting that useful intelligence per watt keeps rising fast. AI Investor's math: call it 15 GW by end-2027, so SpaceX adds about 12 GW in 2027, mostly Nvidia Vera Rubin. At about $40B per gigawatt he puts that at roughly $438B of Nvidia revenue, and doubts Jensen can even find that much supply for Elon next year. He also asked Elon twice where the DRAM and HBM memory for all this will come from.

He bought memory on last week's dip (~12:16 AM ET Oct 21)

"Took some advantage of Elon's FUD on memory last week," quoting his Oct 16 portfolio update (the paywalled "Portfolio Updates - new stock" post). Earlier he mocked the bear case with a sarcastic list of every macro risk and a "fair" memory P/E of 2x, ending "Ok bears, go back to sleep!"

Citi on SK Hynix: memory shortage through 2028 (~1:02 PM ET)

Citi's Q3 2026 preview for SK Hynix: revenue about 101.2T won (+28% vs Q2), operating profit about 81.3T won (+34%), about 8% above the 75.5T consensus. DRAM selling prices up about 28% and NAND up about 24% quarter over quarter. Enterprise SSD demand seen up about 52.9% next year as AI inference and continual learning need more storage. Citi keeps a 3M won target and sees the memory shortage lasting into 2028. He highlighted Citi's expected total return of 137%.

Micron restarts US indium refining (~9:13 PM ET)

Micron is funding Indium Corporation to restart and expand refining of indium, gallium, germanium and tin in Rome, NY, with a long-term supply deal for Micron. China produces nearly 70% of the world's indium. It's part of Micron's plan (announced July) to invest up to $3B in the US chip supply chain. Amount not disclosed.

OpenAI racing to raise $30B at $1.4T (~12:38 PM ET)

Reuters: OpenAI wants about $30B at a valuation above $1.4T signed before Anthropic's expected listing in mid-November. SoftBank and MGX in talks. OpenAI says annualized revenue hit $50B after GPT 6 Astra and is pacing toward $70B by year-end; Anthropic had about $65B annualized by July. His read: the compute race is now fought on balance sheets, backed by real revenue.

Tesla: why he's still out (~2:22 AM ET Oct 21)

He "feels a bit sorry" for Tesla shareholders, who missed almost the entire AI boom over the past four years. He blames Elon for favoring SpaceX (ownership and control); Tesla owning xAI and building the compute SpaceX is building would likely have doubled the stock. Elon said a SpaceX-Tesla merger would be "a good idea," but the special committees haven't agreed on terms and there's no guarantee. AI Investor thinks a merger makes sense; the question is valuation and how much control Elon keeps. He repeated that he sold TSLA and hasn't bought back, though he's still very bullish long term.

Quick hits

  • Howard Marks (Oct 18, Bloomberg) doesn't see a classic AI bubble: real bubbles need investors blind to risk, and everyone is arguing about bubbles daily. He notes the Nasdaq 100 fell at least 10% this year.
  • He mocked the claim that Meta running Google TPUs for inference ends Nvidia's CUDA moat.
  • Nvidia AI tools at Erlangen cut production-prep engineering work by up to 85% and planning costs by up to 20%.
  • Apple caps iPhone Duo orders at 2 per customer; 2TB units resell on eBay for about $5,000 vs $3,199 retail.
  • TD Cowen raised its Qualcomm target to $200 from $175, the same day Reuters reported global layoffs.
  • One promo for his low-cost community tier (no content).

SEP touch: SpaceX demand math and China's shortage both support the NVDA anchor; his memory buying and Citi's shortage-to-2028 call support the DRAM sleeve. His Tesla view is a reminder he's out of TSLA while the plan holds it as a sized "belief asset." No trade signaled.

AI Investor on X, Oct 21 afternoon to evening: Micron answers the CXMT scare, Jensen's gigawatt math, Tesla earnings

Micron: the 4F2 threat is overblown (Oct 21 analyst call)

Micron's CTO Scott DeBoer said the "4F2" DRAM cell design gives little density benefit over today's 6F2. Micron invented 4F2, studied it for 20 years, and chose not to sell it; 3D DRAM will be the next step instead. This directly answers the Oct 12 news that China's CXMT plans 4F2 DDR5 by end-2026, which had knocked memory stocks down. Roadmap: next DRAM node (1-delta, ~mid-20% denser, aimed at HBM5) and 400+ layer NAND both ramp in 2H 2027; HBM4 is already in high-volume production. Micron sees supply tight for at least two more years: "memory has become the AI bottleneck." Late note (8:11 PM ET): the union at Micron's Taoyuan, Taiwan site walks out Thursday 9 AM for 24 hours, even though the Taichung site signed a deal.

Jensen Huang at GTC Berlin: a gigawatt = $50B to build, $40B/yr revenue

That math is why Nvidia ships pre-built "DSX POD" AI factories: a three-month delay costs a gigawatt site about $10B in lost revenue, and PODs cut install-to-first-tokens from 4-5 months to about one. He thinks Nvidia's deployment-speed innovations are underappreciated.

Tesla Q3 and his "still out" stance

Tesla beat (adj. EPS $0.48 vs $0.43 est; revenue $28.05B; FSD attach rate over 75% of new North American deliveries). He called the FSD number "too good to be true?" and argued a non-Musk Tesla earning this would be worth about $19/share vs ~$386. He was "all in" TSLA during the Twitter sale and says the lesson is Elon favors SpaceX. He'd rather buy Tesla at $100B without Elon than at $1.5T with the Elon premium but none of the premium work.

Quick hits

  • Susquehanna raises AMD target to $620, cuts Coherent to $350 (second cut in a week) ahead of Q3.
  • Vultr puts 20MW of AMD MI355X in Chennai, the largest AMD AI build in India.
  • Google Cloud plans to scale Nvidia Vera Rubin to as many as 960,000 GPUs; he wondered if Google will sell TPUs externally too.
  • Zuckerberg expects Meta's "Muse" AI to serve billions.

SEP touch: Micron's 4F2 rebuttal removes much of the CXMT worry from his part-6 MU note and supports holding the DRAM sleeve; watch the 24-hour Taoyuan walkout. Jensen's math supports the NVDA anchor. No trade signaled.

Educational analysis, not professional financial advice.
